The phase portrait for a system of linear differential equations whose matrix has two real, distinct eigenvalues is shown above.
The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[-1,\text{ }3]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively.

before.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-3x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/ed058963b391a4cdc66b2ab48483906a4d07759681c1f24e47ffc9e10775895f.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/6c92028370c86431ddc6ccd9513c273054d98b5add159e1bddf5a2e11751d987.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[−13]andc2eλ2t[11].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[−13] has the equation y=−3x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[−13] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v2=[11] has the equation y=x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[11] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvector [-1,3]^T has slope -3. Along y=-3x, arrows point toward the origin, so solutions decay to the origin and λ₁<0. The eigenvector [1,1]^T has slope 1. Along y=x, arrows point away from the origin, so nonzero solutions grow without bound (the displayed choice 'infinity') and λ₂>0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvector [-1,3]^T gives slope 3/(-1)=-3, so the line is y=-3x. Its arrows point toward the origin, so the eigenvector solutions decay to the origin as t→∞. Thus λ₁<0.

observation.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-3x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/ed058963b391a4cdc66b2ab48483906a4d07759681c1f24e47ffc9e10775895f.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/6c92028370c86431ddc6ccd9513c273054d98b5add159e1bddf5a2e11751d987.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-3x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/ed058963b391a4cdc66b2ab48483906a4d07759681c1f24e47ffc9e10775895f.png)

${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x,
$$

${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

content.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-3x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/ed058963b391a4cdc66b2ab48483906a4d07759681c1f24e47ffc9e10775895f.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/6c92028370c86431ddc6ccd9513c273054d98b5add159e1bddf5a2e11751d987.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

decision.explanation: The eigenpairs give exponential factors e^{4t} and e^{3t}, with eigenvector lines y=-x/2 and y=0. Both exponentials tend to infinity, so nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound. Since e^{3t}/e^{4t}=e^{-t}→0, λ₁=4 dominates and solutions with c₁≠0 become parallel to v₁. Solutions with c₁=0 remain on the horizontal eigenvector line; the zero solution stays at the origin.

observation.name: Question 2
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[2,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

decision.explanation: Each eigenpair (λ,v) gives a solution e^{λt}v. Thus the eigenvector [2,-1]^T is multiplied by e^{4t}, and [1,0]^T by e^{3t}. Their independence makes their linear combination the general solution.

observation.name: Question 2
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[2,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

decision.explanation: Each eigenpair (λ,v) gives a solution e^{λt}v. Thus the eigenvector [2,-1]^T is multiplied by e^{4t}, and [1,0]^T by e^{3t}. Their independence makes their linear combination the general solution.

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[2,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T},$ respectively. $$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

y={{field-3}}

${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

decision.explanation: Eigenpairs give the factors e^{4t} and e^{3t}. The vector [2,-1]^T has slope -1/2. Since e^{4t} tends to positive infinity, every nonzero straight-line solution on this eigenvector line grows without bound, matching 'infinity'. The special case c₁=0 stays at the origin.

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues give exponential factors e^{4t} and e^{3t}. The vector [2,-1]^T has slope -1/2, and e^{4t}→∞, so its nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound. The vector [1,0]^T is horizontal, so its line through the origin is y=0. Zero coefficients give the stationary origin solution.

decision.explanation: The eigenpairs give factors e^{4t} and e^{3t}. Their eigenvector lines are y=-x/2 and y=0. Both exponential factors tend to positive infinity, so nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound, matching the choice 'infinity'. A zero coefficient gives the stationary origin solution.

observation.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/1d2a232b4351c84871d89ba25384aa53777760355ceea6458b07fba9c0a9ed78.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/122759a459c8dd56dbe69c44c0da4ccffbbc660465fbedc7457e17b42430436e.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
0<{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ is the dominant eigenvalue.

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$  solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector  ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/fcaa3ba63a1e6ad061eecf1f72caf3c9f8ba78b014eff044ee5be682e1325128.png)

decision.explanation: The eigenpairs give exponential factors e^{4t} and e^{3t}, with eigenvector lines y=-x/2 and y=0. Both exponentials tend to infinity, so nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound. Since e^{3t}/e^{4t}=e^{-t}→0, λ₁=4 dominates and solutions with c₁≠0 become parallel to v₁. Solutions with c₁=0 remain on the horizontal eigenvector line; the zero solution stays at the origin.

after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/1d2a232b4351c84871d89ba25384aa53777760355ceea6458b07fba9c0a9ed78.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/122759a459c8dd56dbe69c44c0da4ccffbbc660465fbedc7457e17b42430436e.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
0<{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ is the dominant eigenvalue.

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$  solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector  ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$

$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/97f7eb1fbddcd9d927447978efd4c42e705d6835bf0cc74525d42ded8c35346b.png)

${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/edc697ab38ae9a56d46181e0a45982b7045224de0cc3c4a786ddbc515f22196c.png)

must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[21]andc2eλ2t[−11].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[21] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[−11] has the equation y=−x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[−11] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector v1 as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is λ1.

Therefore, λ1>λ2>0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvector lines have slopes 1/2 and -1. Arrows on both point away from the origin, so nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound and both eigenvalues are positive. The curved trajectories become parallel to y=x/2 as they move outward, identifying v₁ as the dominant direction. Therefore λ₁>λ₂>0.

decision.explanation: The vector [2,1]^T has slope 1/2, giving y=x/2. The arrows along this line point away from the origin, so nonzero solutions grow without bound ('infinity') as t→∞. Therefore λ₁>0.

decision.explanation: The eigenvectors give slopes 1/2 and -1, so their lines are y=x/2 and y=-x. Arrows on both lines point away from the origin. Thus nonzero eigenvector solutions grow without bound ('infinity'), requiring λ₁>0 and λ₂>0.

observation.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/97f7eb1fbddcd9d927447978efd4c42e705d6835bf0cc74525d42ded8c35346b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/edc697ab38ae9a56d46181e0a45982b7045224de0cc3c4a786ddbc515f22196c.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[−11] has the equation y=−x, as shown below.

decision.explanation: The eigenvector lines have slopes 1/2 and -1. Arrows on both point away from the origin, so nonzero straight-line solutions grow without bound and both eigenvalues are positive. The curved trajectories become parallel to y=x/2 as they move outward, identifying v₁ as the dominant direction. Therefore λ₁>λ₂>0.

after.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/97f7eb1fbddcd9d927447978efd4c42e705d6835bf0cc74525d42ded8c35346b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/edc697ab38ae9a56d46181e0a45982b7045224de0cc3c4a786ddbc515f22196c.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>0.$

EXPLANATION

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[21]andc2eλ2t[−11].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[21] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[−11] has the equation y=−x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[−11] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector v1 as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is λ1.

Therefore, λ1>λ2>0.
